title: Professional Attire & Dress Etiquette
tagline: Learn what to wear at work and why, build a smart wardrobe on a budget, then dress with confidence, respect and fairness for every occasion.
takeaways: Build a smart wardrobe on a budget
Set fair dress codes as a manager
description:
What you wear speaks before you do. It tells an interviewer you prepared, tells a client you respect them and, in a workshop, can keep you safe. Good attire is not about expensive clothes or a certain body. It is about clothes that are clean, neat, suitable and comfortable for the job and the moment.

**Basic stages (free):**

- **Why attire matters:** first impressions, respect, safety and representing your organisation, and how to read a dress code.
- **A smart wardrobe on a budget:** fit, colours, care, ironing and shoes, for Western business wear and local wear such as shalwar kameez, kurta, waistcoat, dupatta and abaya.
- **Grooming and hygiene:** a simple daily routine that keeps you fresh, even in hot weather.

**Advanced stages (Premium):**

- **Dressing for the occasion:** interviews, client meetings, presentations, video calls, Fridays, weddings, office events and work abroad.
- **Respect and inclusion:** hijab, beards, turbans and other choices, never judging bodies, and dress codes that are fair to everyone.
- **Attire ethics for managers and HR:** writing fair dress codes, giving private and respectful feedback, and safety clothing and PPE.

Follow Maham, a fresh graduate in Lahore, as she gets ready for her first interview and her first job, with help from an HR mentor, a print-shop owner and a site engineer.
audience: Students and fresh graduates getting ready for interviews and a first job
Job seekers and interns who want to look prepared without spending a lot
Office, bank, retail and customer-service staff who meet clients every day
Small-business owners who want their team to look neat and work safely
Team leaders and HR staff who write dress codes or talk to staff about attire
outcomes: Explain why attire matters for first impressions, respect, safety and representing an organisation
Read a dress code and choose suitable formal, business casual, smart casual or uniform outfits
Build a mix-and-match wardrobe of Western and local workwear on a budget and keep it well cared for
Follow a simple daily grooming and hygiene routine, including on hot days
Choose the right outfit for interviews, client meetings, video calls, office events and travel abroad
Respect religious and cultural dress choices and never judge people by their appearance or body
Write fair dress codes, give attire feedback privately and respectfully, and apply PPE rules safely

quest.name: The Ready-to-Work Wardrobe
quest.premise: Maham Siddiqui has just graduated in Lahore and has her first job interview in ten days. She owns one good suit, two lawn suits and a lot of doubts. Her aunt Farah, an HR manager in Karachi, offers to coach her. Along the way Maham meets Danish, who runs a print shop in Faisalabad, his intern Omer, and Jaspal, a site engineer in Peshawar. Clear each stage to build a wardrobe, and a set of habits, that are ready for work.

sessions.title: Why Attire Matters and How to Read a Dress Code
sessions.summary: Discover why clothes matter at work: first impressions, respect, safety and representing your organisation. Then learn to read any dress code, from formal to business casual, smart casual and uniform, and pick a suitable outfit with confidence.
objectives: Explain four reasons attire matters at work in plain words
Tell the difference between formal, business casual, smart casual and uniform dress codes
Read a written dress code and the unwritten signals in a workplace
Choose a suitable outfit when a dress code is unclear

cards.title: Ten days to the interview
cards.setting: Maham's room in Lahore, a video call with her aunt Farah in Karachi.

lines.text: Welcome to The Ready-to-Work Wardrobe. Your first stop is Lahore, where a new graduate has an interview and a big question.
Khala, the email says the interview is at a logistics company and the dress code is 'business casual'. What does that even mean?
Good question, beta. Most people guess. Let us learn to read it properly instead.
Does it mean I need an expensive suit? I only have one, and it is a bit loose now.
No. Good attire is about being clean, neat and suitable. It is not about price, and it is never about your body.
So I can look professional with what I already have?
Very likely. First, let us understand why clothes matter at work at all. Then we will decode that email.

scenes.heading: First impressions
scenes.narration: People notice clothes in the first few seconds. A neat outfit says 'I prepared for this'. It does not decide everything, but it helps you start well.

scenes.heading: Respect
scenes.narration: Dressing suitably shows respect for the people you meet and the occasion, just as you would dress with care for a family elder's dua or a wedding.

scenes.heading: Safety
scenes.narration: In a factory, workshop, hospital or site, clothing protects you. Closed shoes, fitted sleeves and safety gear can prevent injuries.

scenes.heading: Representing the organisation
scenes.narration: When you meet customers, you are the face of your employer. Your appearance becomes part of how people see the whole company.

scenes.heading: Confidence
scenes.narration: Clothes that fit and suit the setting let you stop thinking about yourself and focus on the work and the people.

cards.title: The ladder of formality
cards.caption: Most workplaces sit somewhere on this ladder. Find where yours sits, then dress to match.

items.label: Formal
items.detail: Dark suit and tie, or a formal shalwar kameez with waistcoat; for women a suit, formal kurta or shalwar kameez with dupatta, or a smart abaya.

items.label: Business formal
items.detail: Suit or blazer with formal trousers or skirt, or neat formal local wear in plain colours.

items.label: Business casual
items.detail: Collared shirt or blouse with trousers, a neat kurta, or a plain shalwar kameez. Blazer optional, tie usually not needed.

items.label: Smart casual
items.detail: Neat polo shirts, simple tops, clean chinos, lawn suits and tidy shoes. Relaxed but still neat.

items.label: Casual
items.detail: Everyday comfortable clothes. Rare at work, except on some dress-down days.

cards.question: Maham's email says the interview dress code is 'business casual'. Which outfit fits best?
options: A sparkly party outfit, because an interview is a special event
A T-shirt and jeans, because 'casual' is in the name
A pressed collared shirt or neat kurta with trousers, or a plain shalwar kameez with dupatta
A full wedding sherwani, to be extra formal
cards.explanation: Business casual is neat and professional without needing a full suit or tie. A pressed shirt or kurta with trousers, or a plain shalwar kameez, fits well. Party and wedding clothes are for other occasions.

cards.title: Attire is a message, not a judgement
cards.body:
Your clothes send a simple message: **I prepared, I respect you, and I understand this setting.**

That message does not need expensive clothes. It needs clothes that are:

- **Clean** and free of stains
- **Neat:** pressed, with no loose threads or missing buttons
- **Suitable** for the dress code and the job
- **Comfortable** enough that you can work well

Attire is also never a judgement of a person's body, skin colour, faith or income. In this course we judge outfits against a setting, never people against a standard of looks.

cards.back: The most dressed-up level: dark suits, ties or formal local wear in plain, deep colours. Common for senior meetings and ceremonies.
Professional but relaxed: collared shirts, blouses, kurtas, neat trousers. A tie or blazer is usually optional.
Neat everyday clothes: polo shirts, simple tops, chinos, lawn suits. Relaxed, but never scruffy.
Clothes the employer chooses so staff look the same and stay safe. Wear it complete, clean and as intended.
A day, often Friday in some offices, when rules relax. Check what 'relaxed' means in your workplace.
A role where you meet customers or partners. These roles often need a slightly more formal look.

cards.title: Business casual or smart casual?
cards.caption: The two most common office codes, side by side.

items.label: Tops
items.right: Polo shirts, simple tops, plain kurtas

items.label: Bottoms
items.left: Formal trousers, knee-length or longer skirts
items.right: Chinos, neat trousers, clean dark jeans where allowed

items.label: Local wear
items.left: Plain shalwar kameez, kurta with trousers, dupatta
items.right: Lawn or cotton suits, kurta with shalwar

items.label: Layers
items.right: Cardigan, light jacket or shawl

items.label: Shoes
items.left: Leather shoes, loafers, closed flats or low heels
items.right: Clean loafers, neat sandals or chappals where allowed

cards.title: First day, no clear rules
cards.situation: Maham gets the job. The welcome email says only 'please dress appropriately'. She has no idea what the team wears, and her first day includes a short meeting with the operations head.

choices.text: Wear a neat business casual outfit, watch what colleagues wear, and ask her manager about the dress code on day one.
choices.outcome: Maham looks prepared, fits in comfortably and learns the real norms by asking politely. This is the safest path.

choices.text: Wear her most formal suit, just in case.
choices.outcome: She looks prepared, though slightly overdressed. That is fine for a first day, but she still needs to find out the norm.

choices.text: Wear jeans and trainers because nobody told her otherwise.
choices.outcome: She feels out of place in the meeting. When a code is unclear, guessing low is riskier than dressing one step up.

cards.title: Where does this outfit belong?
cards.prompt: Sort each outfit into the dress code it suits best.

items.text: Dark suit, white shirt and tie
Formal shalwar kameez with a dark waistcoat
Pressed shirt and formal trousers, no tie
Plain kurta, trousers and dupatta, with closed flats
Neat polo shirt and chinos
Printed lawn suit with simple sandals

cards.question: Danish's print shop gives every worker a fitted shop shirt and closed shoes to wear near the machines. Which reason for attire does this show most clearly?
options: Fashion, so the team looks stylish online
Safety, with representing the shop as a second reason
First impressions only, because customers visit
Saving money on staff salaries
cards.explanation: Fitted clothes and closed shoes reduce the chance of being caught in machines or hurt by dropped items. A matching shop shirt also represents the business, but safety is the main reason here.

cards.title: A uniform with a reason
cards.body:
Danish Akhtar runs a small print shop in Faisalabad. Last year an employee's loose shawl end brushed a moving machine. Nobody was hurt, but it was a close call.

Danish now gives each worker two fitted cotton shop shirts in the shop colour and asks everyone to wear closed shoes. Long scarves or dupattas are pinned or tucked in near machines, and there is a safe locker for anything loose.

He explained the **reason** to the team, not just the rule. Customers now recognise his staff at once, and the team feels safer. One change served two purposes: **safety** and **representing the business**.

cards.title: Why does it matter here?
cards.prompt: Match each situation to the main reason attire matters.

pairs.left: A bank teller wears the bank's uniform at the counter
pairs.right: Representing the organisation

pairs.left: A lab assistant wears a lab coat and closed shoes
pairs.right: Safety

pairs.left: A candidate wears a pressed shirt to an interview
pairs.right: First impressions

pairs.left: A trainee dresses neatly for a senior visitor
pairs.right: Respect for the people and the occasion

cards.title: When in doubt, step up and ask
cards.body:
If you are not sure what to wear, **dress one step more formal** than you think you need. It is easy to remove a blazer or waistcoat; it is hard to look prepared in clothes that are too casual.

Then **ask**. A short message such as 'Could you tell me what the usual dress code is for the team?' is polite and shows you care. HR staff and managers are glad to answer.

cards.title: Take-aways from The Front Door
items: Attire matters for first impressions, respect, safety, representing your organisation and your own confidence.
Good attire means clean, neat, suitable and comfortable. It is not about price or body shape.
Most workplaces sit on a ladder: formal, business formal, business casual, smart casual, casual.
Uniforms and safety clothing are worn complete, clean and as intended.
Read both the written code and what colleagues actually wear.
When unsure, dress one step more formal and ask politely.

cards.prompt: Think of a place where you work, study or want to work. Where does it sit on the ladder of formality? Which outfit you already own would fit it best, and what one change would make it look neater?

quiz.question: Which statement best describes good professional attire?
options: Clothes that are clean, neat, suitable for the setting and comfortable
Clothes that follow the latest trends and come from the most expensive shops in town
Clothes that follow one standard look for every body type
Clothes in bright colours so people remember you
quiz.explanation: Good attire is about being clean, neat, suitable and comfortable. Price, trends and body shape are not the measure.

quiz.question: A job advert says 'business casual'. Which outfit is the safest choice for the interview?
options: Shorts and a sports T-shirt, because comfort matters most on a stressful interview day
Pressed shirt or blouse with formal trousers, or a plain kurta or shalwar kameez
A heavy embroidered wedding outfit
Whatever you wore to university yesterday
quiz.explanation: Business casual means professional but relaxed. A pressed shirt or neat local wear in plain colours fits well.

quiz.question: Why do many factories require closed shoes and fitted sleeves?
options: To make the factory look more modern and organised in photographs for its website and adverts
To make sure all workers look the same height
To protect workers from injuries such as crushed toes or clothes caught in machines
To stop workers from taking breaks
quiz.explanation: In workshops and factories, clothing is part of safety. Closed shoes protect feet and fitted sleeves reduce the risk of getting caught in moving parts.

quiz.question: Which outfit belongs to the smart casual level, not formal?
options: A neat polo shirt with chinos
A dark suit with a tie
A formal shalwar kameez with a dark waistcoat
A matching blazer suit with formal trousers
quiz.explanation: Polo shirts and chinos are neat but relaxed, which is smart casual. Suits, ties and formal waistcoat outfits sit at the formal end.

quiz.question: A welcome email says only 'dress appropriately'. What should a new employee do first?
options: Wear casual clothes for the first few weeks and wait until someone complains about them
Copy an outfit from a social media influencer
Dress neatly in business casual, observe colleagues and ask the manager about the norm
Skip the first meeting until the rules are clear
quiz.explanation: When the code is unclear, a neat business casual outfit is safe, and asking politely tells you the real norm.

quiz.question: What does it mean to say an employee 'represents the organisation' through attire?
options: The employee must buy all work clothes from the company's own shop and wear its logo daily
Customers see the employee's appearance as part of how the company looks and behaves
The employee's clothes are owned by the company
The employee must wear the company logo outside work
quiz.explanation: In client-facing roles, people judge the company partly by how its staff look. That is why many firms ask for neat attire or a uniform.

quiz.question: Which is the best reason to dress one step more formal when you are unsure?
options: Formal clothes are always more comfortable than casual clothes, whatever the weather or the job
Managers give higher pay to the most formal dressers
It is easy to remove a layer, but hard to look prepared in clothes that are too casual
Casual clothes are not allowed in any workplace
quiz.explanation: Dressing one step up keeps your options open: a blazer or waistcoat can come off. Being too casual is harder to fix on the day.

quiz.question: A trainee bank officer is given a uniform jacket but wears it with the sleeves rolled up and a stain on the front. What is the main problem?
options: A uniform should be worn complete, clean and as intended, because it represents the bank
Uniforms are optional, so there is no problem
He should have bought a more expensive jacket
The jacket colour does not suit his skin tone
quiz.explanation: A uniform shows customers that staff belong to the organisation. Stains and careless wearing weaken that message. It is about care, not cost or looks.

quiz.question: Which question helps most when reading the unwritten dress code of a new workplace?
options: What do people in similar roles wear on a normal day and when meeting clients?
What is the most expensive outfit anyone in the office wears, so that I can match or beat it?
Which colleague has the most followers online?
What did the company wear in photos from ten years ago?
quiz.explanation: Watching people in similar roles, on normal days and client days, shows how the written code is applied in practice.

quiz.question: Farah says 'attire is a message, not a judgement'. What does she mean?
options: Only people who dress well deserve respect, so managers should rank staff by their clothes
Managers should rate staff on how attractive they look
Clothes do not matter at all in any workplace
Clothes show care for the setting, but never measure a person's worth, body or faith
quiz.explanation: Attire communicates care and suitability. It must never be used to judge someone's body, skin colour, faith or income.

sessions.title: Building a Smart Wardrobe on a Budget
sessions.summary: Build a small, mix-and-match work wardrobe that fits well and lasts. Learn to check fit, choose a calm colour base, combine Western business wear with local wear such as shalwar kameez, kurta, waistcoat, dupatta and abaya, and care for clothes and shoes so they always look fresh.
objectives: Check the fit of shirts, trousers, kameez and jackets with simple tests
Plan a mix-and-match wardrobe around a few neutral colours
Combine Western business wear and local wear for different dress codes
Wash, iron and store clothes and care for shoes so they last longer
Spend a small budget where it makes the biggest difference

cards.title: One suit and a lot of doubts
cards.setting: Maham's cupboard in Lahore, Saturday afternoon. Omer joins the video call from Faisalabad.

lines.text: Stage two. Maham opens her cupboard to plan a week of work outfits, and finds more questions than clothes.
I have one dark suit, two printed lawn suits, some shirts and a pair of black flats. That is not a work wardrobe.
I am worse. My internship starts next month and all my shirts are either too big or have faded collars.
You both have more than you think. A work wardrobe is not about many clothes. It is about a few that fit and mix well.
But I have only a small amount of money saved.
Then we spend it where it matters most: fit, shoes and care. Let us start with the fit test.

cards.title: Five steps to a smart wardrobe

scenes.heading: Fit first
scenes.narration: A simple piece that fits well looks better than an expensive one that does not. Check shoulders, sleeves, length and room to move.

scenes.heading: A calm colour base
scenes.narration: Choose a few neutral colours such as navy, grey, black, white, cream and light blue. They mix easily, so a few pieces make many outfits.

scenes.heading: Mix and match
scenes.narration: Every top should go with at least two bottoms. A waistcoat, blazer, shawl or dupatta changes the look without new outfits.

scenes.heading: Care
scenes.narration: Washing gently, ironing properly and hanging clothes straight away keeps them looking new for much longer.

scenes.heading: Shoes
scenes.narration: Clean, polished, comfortable shoes finish any outfit. People notice tired shoes more than you expect.

cards.title: The mix-and-match wardrobe
cards.caption: Build from the bottom up. Most of your money goes on the base layer.

items.label: A few accents
items.detail: One or two patterned dupattas, ties, scarves or shawls to add colour.

items.label: Layers
items.detail: A blazer, a waistcoat, a cardigan or a plain shawl that change the level of formality.

items.label: Core tops
items.detail: Plain shirts, blouses, kurtas and kameez in light neutral colours.

items.label: Base pieces
items.detail: Well-fitting trousers, shalwar and comfortable shoes in dark neutral colours.

cards.back: The shoulder seam sits at the edge of your shoulder, not halfway down your arm or pulling tight.
Shirt and kameez sleeves end around the wrist bone when your arms hang down.
You can slip one or two fingers inside a buttoned collar without it feeling tight.
They sit comfortably at the waist and the hem just touches the top of your shoes, not dragging on the floor.
You can sit, reach and bend without buttons pulling or fabric straining.
Choose a length that is comfortable and modest for you and the setting. Hems should be even.

cards.question: Omer's new shirt has shoulder seams that hang halfway down his upper arms. What is the best advice?
options: Keep it, because loose shirts always look more formal
Roll up the sleeves so nobody notices
Wear a tie to hide the problem
Choose a smaller size or have it altered, because the shoulders do not fit
cards.explanation: Shoulders are the hardest part to alter and the first sign of poor fit. A smaller size, or a tailor's help if possible, will make the shirt look much neater.

cards.title: Western and local business wear
cards.caption: Both are professional. Choose what suits the dress code, your role and your own choice.

items.label: Formal
items.left: Dark suit, shirt and tie, or a trouser or skirt suit
items.right: Plain shalwar kameez with a dark waistcoat; formal kameez or kurta with dupatta or a smart abaya

items.label: Business casual
items.left: Collared shirt or blouse with formal trousers
items.right: Plain kurta with trousers or shalwar; cotton suit with dupatta

items.label: Layers
items.right: Waistcoat, shawl, plain abaya or long coat

items.label: Shoes
items.left: Leather shoes, loafers, closed flats or low heels
items.right: Leather shoes, neat chappals or khussas where allowed

items.label: Colours
items.left: Navy, grey, black, white, light blue
items.right: White, cream, grey, navy, soft pastels and earth tones

cards.title: Fabrics for Pakistani weather
cards.body:
Our weather changes a lot between seasons and cities, so fabric matters.

- **Summer:** cotton and lawn breathe well and absorb sweat. Light colours stay cooler in the sun.
- **Winter:** khaddar, wool blends and warm layers such as a waistcoat, cardigan, shawl or blazer keep you warm while still looking neat.
- **All year:** plain or softly patterned fabrics look more professional than shiny or heavily embroidered ones, which are better kept for weddings and events.

Always read the **care label** before buying. A fabric that needs dry cleaning every time may cost more in the long run than one you can wash at home.

cards.title: Omer's internship budget
cards.situation: Omer has saved a small amount for his internship clothes. A shop assistant shows him one stylish suit that would use all of it. He could instead buy two plain shirts, one pair of well-fitting trousers and get his old shoes resoled and polished.

choices.text: Buy the plain shirts and trousers, fix and polish his shoes, and wear his one good kurta and waistcoat on other days.
choices.outcome: Omer has several neat outfits for every day of the week. They fit, mix easily and his shoes look cared for. This is the smart choice.

choices.text: Buy the stylish suit and wear it every day.
choices.outcome: He looks sharp on the first day, but the suit wears out quickly and he has nothing to change into. One piece is not a wardrobe.

choices.text: Buy two cheap shirts in bright fashion colours that do not match his trousers.
choices.outcome: He has more clothes, but they do not mix well and look less professional. Colour planning matters as much as quantity.

cards.title: Iron a shirt the neat way
cards.prompt: Put these steps for ironing a shirt or kameez in a sensible order.
steps: Check the care label and set the iron to the right heat for the fabric
Iron the collar, both sides, from the points towards the middle
Iron the cuffs, then the sleeves
Iron the shoulders and the back
Iron the front panels, working carefully around buttons
Hang it straight away on a hanger and fasten the top button

cards.title: Spend or save?
cards.prompt: Sort each item by whether it is usually worth spending a little more on, or easy to save on.

items.text: Comfortable, well-made shoes you wear every day
Tailoring to fix the fit of trousers or a kameez
Trendy pieces that will look dated next year
Many accessories that you rarely wear
A plain blazer or waistcoat that goes with everything
A fourth outfit in a colour that matches nothing else

cards.question: Maham owns a navy kurta, a white blouse, black trousers, a grey shalwar and one dark suit. Which purchase adds the most new outfits?
options: A plain cream kameez that goes with both the black trousers and the grey shalwar
A bright orange top that only matches one printed dupatta
Another dark suit almost the same as the one she has
A heavily embroidered party dress for weddings
cards.explanation: A neutral top that mixes with several existing bottoms creates more outfits. Items that match nothing, or repeat what you have, add little.

cards.title: Care that makes clothes last
cards.prompt: Match each care problem to a good habit.

pairs.left: Dark clothes look shiny after ironing
pairs.right: Iron them inside out or with a thin cloth on top

pairs.left: White shirts turn grey over time
pairs.right: Wash whites separately and do not overload the machine

pairs.left: Sweat marks on collars
pairs.right: Wash soon after wearing and treat the collar gently

pairs.left: Leather shoes crack and look tired
pairs.right: Clean and polish them often and let them rest a day between wears

pairs.left: Clothes crease in the cupboard
pairs.right: Hang shirts and kameez straight away, with space between hangers

cards.title: Maham's ten-piece work week
cards.body:
Maham listed what she owned and added just two pieces: a plain cream kameez and a navy cardigan.

- **Monday:** white blouse, black trousers, navy cardigan, black flats
- **Tuesday:** navy kurta, grey shalwar, plain dupatta
- **Wednesday:** dark suit for the client meeting
- **Thursday:** cream kameez, black trousers, plain dupatta
- **Friday:** cream kameez, grey shalwar, navy cardigan

Ten pieces, five different outfits, all in calm colours that mix. Each evening she checks the next day's outfit for stains and loose buttons and irons it, so mornings are calm.

cards.title: Shoes finish the outfit
cards.body:
- Keep work shoes **clean and polished**; a quick wipe each evening helps.
- Choose **closed, comfortable shoes** for long days and anywhere with safety rules.
- Low heels, flats, loafers and leather shoes all work in offices. Comfort matters.
- Match **socks to trousers** in dark colours with formal wear.
- Neat **chappals or khussas** can suit local wear where the dress code allows it, but check first for client meetings and sites.

cards.title: Take-aways from The Wardrobe Workshop
items: Fit comes first: check shoulders, sleeves, collar, length and room to move.
Build on a few neutral colours so a small wardrobe makes many outfits.
Western business wear and local wear are both professional when they are neat and suit the dress code.
Choose breathable cotton and lawn in summer and warm neat layers in winter.
Read care labels, iron properly and hang clothes straight away.
Spend on fit, shoes and versatile layers; save on trends and extras.

cards.prompt: List the work-suitable clothes you own today. How many outfits can you make from them? Which single piece in a neutral colour would add the most new combinations?

quiz.question: Where should the shoulder seam of a well-fitting shirt sit?
options: At the edge of the shoulder
Halfway down the upper arm
Close to the neck
Wherever is most comfortable when lying down
quiz.explanation: A shoulder seam at the edge of the shoulder is the clearest sign of good fit. Shoulders are also hard to alter, so check them first.

quiz.question: Why do neutral colours such as navy, grey, white and cream help a small wardrobe?
options: They are the only colours allowed by most offices, so you avoid breaking the rules
They are the only colours allowed in offices
They make every outfit formal
They mix easily, so a few pieces make many different outfits
quiz.explanation: Neutral colours combine with almost everything, which multiplies the outfits you can make from a few pieces.

quiz.question: Which fabric is usually the most comfortable for a hot summer workday in Lahore or Karachi?
options: Light cotton or lawn
Heavy wool
Shiny synthetic fabric
Thick khaddar
quiz.explanation: Cotton and lawn breathe and absorb sweat, which keeps you cooler. Wool and khaddar suit winter.

quiz.question: What should you do before setting the iron's heat?
options: Spray perfume on the fabric
Read the clothing's care label
Set it to the highest heat for every fabric
Wet the whole garment completely
quiz.explanation: The care label tells you the safe heat for the fabric. Too much heat can burn or shine delicate fabrics.

quiz.question: Which item is usually worth spending a little more on?
options: A trendy colour that will look dated next year
A fourth outfit that matches nothing else
Many accessories you rarely wear
Comfortable, well-made shoes you wear every day
quiz.explanation: Shoes are worn daily and affect both comfort and appearance. Spending on items you wear often gives the best value.

quiz.question: Which outfit is a suitable business casual choice in local wear?
options: A heavily embroidered wedding outfit with sequins, since it shows you made a real effort
Sports clothes with a shawl on top
A sleeping kurta with slippers
A plain kurta with trousers or shalwar, or a cotton suit with dupatta
quiz.explanation: Plain, neat local wear in calm colours fits business casual. Heavy embroidery and sequins are better kept for events.

quiz.question: Omer's trousers drag on the floor behind his heels. What is the simplest fix?
options: Wear them pulled up higher above the waist all day, so the hems lift off the floor
Have the hem shortened so it just touches the top of his shoes
Roll them up twice at the ankle
Buy a much larger size so they look loose on purpose
quiz.explanation: A tailor can shorten a hem quickly. Trousers and shalwar look neatest when the hem just touches the top of the shoes.

quiz.question: Dark trousers look shiny after ironing. What is the best habit?
options: Iron them at the highest heat for longer
Stop ironing dark clothes completely
Add more starch each time
Iron them inside out or with a thin cloth on top
quiz.explanation: The shine comes from direct heat pressing the fabric. Ironing inside out or through a cloth prevents it.

quiz.question: Maham owns black trousers, a grey shalwar and a navy cardigan. Which new piece gives her the most new outfits?
options: A bright pink top that matches only one dupatta
A second pair of black trousers just like the first
A plain cream kameez that matches all three
A heavy party dress
quiz.explanation: A neutral piece that works with several items you already own creates the most combinations.

quiz.question: Farah says 'fit, shoes and care' matter more than the number of clothes. Which reason is strongest?
options: Managers count how many different outfits each staff member owns when deciding on promotions
Owning fewer clothes means you never need to wash them
Shoes are the only thing people look at
A few well-fitting, cared-for pieces look better than many that do not fit
quiz.explanation: People notice fit, condition and neatness. A small, cared-for wardrobe gives a polished look every day.

sessions.title: Grooming and Hygiene Basics
sessions.summary: Build a simple daily grooming routine that keeps you clean, fresh and confident, whatever your style, faith or budget. Learn the basics of bathing, oral care, hair and beard care, nails, fragrance and staying fresh on hot days, and how to plan your outfit the night before.
objectives: Follow a simple morning and evening grooming routine
Keep hair, beards, nails and breath neat and fresh
Stay fresh on hot days and long commutes
Use fragrance and make-up lightly, as personal choices
Separate real grooming needs from myths and personal style

cards.title: The hot commute
cards.setting: A rickshaw stop in Lahore, a June morning. Maham calls Farah on the way to her second interview.

lines.text: Stage three. Maham's outfit is ready, but the June heat has its own plans.
Khala, I left home fresh, but after twenty minutes in this heat I feel sticky. The interview is in half an hour!
Breathe. This happens to everyone in our summers. Do you have tissues and a small bottle of water?
Yes, and a comb and deodorant in my bag, like you said.
Then you are ready. Find the washroom, freshen up for five minutes and walk in calm. Good grooming is a habit, not a miracle.
Farah ji told me you were nervous. On site in Peshawar we start at seven in the heat. A small kit in the bag saves the day every time.
Then today I will build my own routine.

scenes.heading: Clean body
scenes.narration: A daily bath or shower, and deodorant or antiperspirant afterwards, are the base of feeling fresh all day.

scenes.heading: Fresh breath
scenes.narration: Brush your teeth morning and night and rinse after meals. Carry water; a dry mouth makes breath worse.

scenes.heading: Neat hair and beard
scenes.narration: Any hairstyle or beard can be professional when it is clean and tidy. Choose your style; keep it groomed.

scenes.heading: Clean hands and nails
scenes.narration: People see your hands when you shake hands, write or type. Keep nails clean and trimmed to a neat length.

scenes.heading: Fresh clothes
scenes.narration: Wear clean clothes each day, especially shirts, kameez and socks. Air jackets and waistcoats between wears.

cards.title: The daily grooming cycle
cards.caption: Small steps at the same times each day become an easy habit.

items.label: Morning
items.detail: Bath or shower, deodorant, teeth, hair and beard, clean clothes.

items.label: Before you leave
items.detail: Mirror check: collar, buttons, dupatta or tie, shoes, and your small kit in the bag.

items.label: Midday
items.detail: Wash hands and face, rinse your mouth after lunch, comb hair.

items.label: Evening
items.detail: Brush teeth, hang or wash today's clothes, wipe your shoes.

items.label: Night before
items.detail: Choose and iron tomorrow's outfit and check it for stains or loose buttons.

cards.question: Which statement about beards at work is accurate?
options: Only clean-shaven men look professional
A clean, groomed beard of any length can be fully professional
Beards must always be cut very short in every job
Beards are only allowed on Fridays
cards.explanation: Many people keep beards for faith, culture or choice. What matters is that it is clean and groomed. Some safety roles need a close fit for certain masks, which employers should handle respectfully and offer alternatives where possible.

cards.back: Fact: soap, water, a toothbrush, a comb, nail clippers and clean clothes cover most of it.

cards.front: Myth: strong perfume means you are clean
cards.back: Fact: fragrance covers smells for a while but does not replace washing. Strong scents can bother colleagues.

cards.front: Myth: women must wear make-up at work
cards.back: Fact: make-up is a personal choice. A clean, neat appearance is professional with or without it.
Fact: hair of any length is professional when clean and tidy. Tie it back where safety needs it.
Fact: a clean, groomed beard is professional, and many people keep one for faith or choice.

cards.title: Fragrance and make-up: light and personal
cards.body:
**Fragrance** is a personal choice. If you use perfume or attar, use a little. Many people work close together in offices, cars and lifts, and some colleagues have allergies, asthma or headaches triggered by strong scents. A good test: someone should only notice it if they are close to you.

**Make-up** is also a choice, for any gender. If you wear it, a light, neat look usually suits the daytime office. No one should be required to wear it, and no one should be judged for wearing it or not.

The same idea applies to jewellery and accessories: simple and quiet usually works best at work, and some jobs need fewer items for safety.

cards.title: Fresh habit or common slip?
cards.prompt: Sort each habit by whether it keeps you fresh at work or is a common slip.

items.text: Rinsing your mouth after lunch
Wearing yesterday's shirt again after a hot day
Carrying tissues, a comb and deodorant in your bag
Using a lot of strong perfume instead of bathing
Trimming and cleaning nails each week
Ignoring a stain because 'nobody will notice'
Airing your waistcoat or jacket between wears

cards.title: Quick wins first
cards.caption: Start with the habits that take little effort but make a big difference.

items.label: Quick wins
items.detail: Clean nails, fresh breath, combed hair, a wiped pair of shoes.

items.label: Worth the effort
items.detail: Ironing tomorrow's outfit the night before, a weekly beard or hair trim.

items.label: Small touches
items.detail: A neat handkerchief, a matching hair tie or pin.

items.label: Usually not needed
items.detail: Long, costly beauty routines just for work.

cards.title: Five minutes before the interview
cards.situation: Maham reaches the office twenty-five minutes early. She feels hot and sticky, her dupatta has slipped and her shoes are dusty from the street.

choices.text: Ask for the washroom, wash her face and hands, use deodorant, fix her dupatta, wipe her shoes and sit calmly to wait.
choices.outcome: Maham feels fresh and composed when she is called in. Planning a small kit and arriving early made this easy.

choices.text: Spray a lot of perfume and go straight in.
choices.outcome: The strong scent fills the small interview room and the panel is distracted. Fragrance does not replace freshening up.

choices.text: Wait in the lobby and hope nobody notices.
choices.outcome: She stays uncomfortable and keeps thinking about it during the interview. A few minutes of freshening up would have helped her focus.

cards.title: A calm morning routine
cards.prompt: Put these morning steps in a sensible order.
steps: Wake up with enough time; do not rush
Bath or shower, then deodorant
Brush teeth and groom hair and beard
Put on the outfit you ironed the night before
Mirror check: collar, buttons, dupatta or tie, shoes
Check your bag for your small grooming kit

cards.question: A colleague uses a very strong perfume and another colleague gets headaches. What is the best general rule for fragrance at work?
options: Use as much as you like, because it shows you are clean
Never wash on days you wear perfume
Use a little, so only someone close to you can notice it
Spray perfume on the shared office chairs
cards.explanation: Light fragrance is a reasonable personal choice, but strong scents can affect people with allergies, asthma or migraines. A little goes a long way.

cards.title: Jaspal's site-day kit
cards.body:
Jaspal Singh is a site engineer in Peshawar. He starts early and spends hours outdoors.

His routine: a morning shower, deodorant, teeth, and time to tie his turban neatly and groom his beard. His small bag holds tissues, a comb, a small towel, deodorant, a toothbrush, a spare vest and a bottle of water.

Before a client visit at the site office, he takes five minutes to wash his face and hands, change his vest and wipe his safety boots. 'The site is dusty,' he says, 'but I can still meet the client looking cared for.' His faith-based turban and beard are part of his professional look, kept neat like everything else.

cards.title: Grooming item and its job
cards.prompt: Match each item in a small grooming kit to what it helps with.

pairs.left: Deodorant
pairs.right: Staying fresh after a hot commute

pairs.left: Comb or hairbrush
pairs.right: Tidying hair after wind, a helmet or a long ride

pairs.left: Water bottle
pairs.right: Avoiding a dry mouth and staying cool

pairs.left: Tissues or a small towel
pairs.right: Wiping sweat and dust before a meeting

pairs.left: Nail clippers at home
pairs.right: Keeping hands neat for handshakes and typing

cards.title: Be kind about hygiene
cards.body:
Hygiene can be affected by many things: a long commute, a health condition, a lack of running water at home or simply a very hot day. If you ever notice a problem in a colleague, never mock or gossip. In stage six we look at how managers can raise it privately and kindly.

For yourself, aim for **steady habits, not perfection**. A small kit and a routine solve most problems.

cards.title: Take-aways from The Mirror Room
items: Daily basics: bath or shower, deodorant, teeth, neat hair and beard, clean nails, clean clothes.
Any hairstyle, beard or head covering is professional when it is clean and neat.
Fragrance and make-up are personal choices; use them lightly at work.
Carry a small kit on hot days: tissues, comb, deodorant, water.
Plan and iron tomorrow's outfit the night before for calm mornings.
Be kind about hygiene; never mock or gossip about anyone's appearance.

cards.prompt: Which part of your current routine is easiest to improve this week? Write down what you would put in your own small grooming kit for a hot day.

quiz.question: What is the base of staying fresh during a workday?
options: A large amount of perfume
Changing shoes three times a day
A daily bath or shower followed by deodorant
Wearing only white clothes
quiz.explanation: Washing and deodorant are the foundation. Fragrance does not replace them.

quiz.question: Which statement about hair at work is accurate?
options: Only short hair is professional, so long hair should be cut before starting an office job
Long hair must always be cut for office jobs
Hair must be coloured to look neat
Hair of any length or style is professional when it is clean and tidy
quiz.explanation: Style is personal. What matters is that hair is clean and neat, and tied back where safety requires it.

quiz.question: Why is it wise to use only a little fragrance at work?
options: Strong scents can bother colleagues, including people with allergies
Perfume is not allowed in any country's offices, so using it could break the law at work
Fragrance stains every type of fabric
Light fragrance is more expensive
quiz.explanation: Offices, cars and lifts are shared spaces. A little fragrance is fine; strong scents can make others unwell.

quiz.question: Which item is most useful in a small grooming kit for a hot day?
options: A full set of party make-up
A second pair of formal shoes
Tissues, a comb, deodorant and water
A large bottle of strong perfume
quiz.explanation: A light kit helps you freshen up quickly after a commute or before a meeting.

quiz.question: Is make-up required to look professional at work?
options: Yes, for all women in every job, because a bare face looks tired to clients
Yes, but only for men in sales
No, it is a personal choice for anyone
No, it is banned in all offices
quiz.explanation: No one should be required to wear make-up, and no one should be judged for wearing it or not.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of ironing tomorrow's outfit the night before?
options: Clothes last twice as long
Managers check outfits every evening
Mornings are calmer and you can fix stains or loose buttons in time
Clothes do not need washing afterwards
quiz.explanation: Preparing the evening before removes stress and gives you time to fix problems.

quiz.question: Which habit is a common grooming slip?
options: Wearing yesterday's shirt again after a hot, sweaty day
Rinsing your mouth after lunch
Airing a waistcoat between wears
Trimming nails each week
quiz.explanation: Shirts, kameez and socks absorb sweat and should be washed after a hot day. The other habits keep you fresh.

quiz.question: Maham arrives at an interview hot and dusty with twenty minutes to spare. What is the best use of the time?
options: Spray a lot of perfume, skip the washroom and go straight in so she is not late
Freshen up in the washroom, fix her dupatta, wipe her shoes and wait calmly
Leave and reschedule the interview
Sit and worry about how she looks
quiz.explanation: A few minutes of freshening up restores comfort and confidence, so she can focus on the interview.

quiz.question: Which grooming habit is a quick win: low effort but high impact?
options: A long, costly beauty routine every morning
Keeping nails clean and breath fresh
Buying a new outfit every week
Changing your hairstyle each month
quiz.explanation: Clean nails and fresh breath are noticed in every handshake and conversation, and take very little effort.

quiz.question: A colleague often looks tired and sometimes has a body odour. Based on this stage, what is the right attitude?
options: Make a joke about it in front of the team so they get the message without a serious talk
Stay kind and never gossip; there may be reasons you do not know
Tell the whole team so everyone can help
Avoid sitting near them and say nothing ever
quiz.explanation: Hygiene problems can have many causes. Mocking or gossiping hurts people. A manager can raise it privately and kindly, as stage six explains.

sessions.title: Dressing for the Occasion: Interviews, Clients, Cameras and Travel
sessions.summary: Go beyond the daily dress code and dress for the moment: interviews, client meetings, presentations, video calls, Fridays, colleagues' weddings, office events, business travel and work abroad. Use a simple occasion check to choose the right outfit every time.
objectives: Use the occasion check (who, where, what, weather, work) to choose an outfit
Plan an interview outfit and a presentation outfit step by step
Dress well for video calls, including colours and patterns that work on camera
Handle Fridays, weddings, office events and iftars with suitable attire
Prepare attire for business travel and work abroad by researching local norms

cards.title: Three invitations in one week
cards.setting: Farah's office in Karachi. Maham, now three months into her job, joins by video.

lines.text: Welcome to the Advanced stages. Maham's job is going well, and her calendar has just become complicated.
Khala, this week I have a client presentation on Tuesday, a video call with our Dubai partner on Thursday, and my colleague's mehndi on Saturday!
Three occasions, three different outfits. The daily dress code is only the starting point.
And Danish sahib has invited me to speak to his team in Faisalabad on Friday. Is Friday more relaxed?
In my shop, many of us wear shalwar kameez on Fridays. But when a guest speaks to the team, we still look neat.
Exactly. Before every event, ask five quick questions. Let me show you the occasion check.

scenes.heading: Who
scenes.narration: Who will you meet? Senior clients, a hiring panel and foreign partners often expect a more formal look than your own team.

scenes.heading: Where
scenes.narration: Office, client site, factory floor, hotel, home or screen? The place changes what is suitable and safe.

scenes.heading: What
scenes.narration: What is the purpose? Persuading, presenting, celebrating or working hands-on each suggest a different outfit.

scenes.heading: Weather
scenes.narration: Heat, rain, cold or long travel affect fabric, layers and shoes. Comfort helps you perform.

scenes.heading: Work role
scenes.narration: Your role in the event matters. A speaker or host usually dresses a step more formal than the audience.

cards.title: Interview day, planned backwards
cards.caption: Good interview attire starts days before the interview.

items.label: A week before
items.detail: Research the company: photos, website and people in similar roles. Decide on one step above their daily code.

items.label: Three days before
items.detail: Try the full outfit on, sit and walk in it, and fix any fit problems or loose buttons.

items.label: The night before
items.detail: Iron the outfit, polish shoes, pack your grooming kit and documents.

items.label: The morning
items.detail: Follow your routine, dress, and leave early enough to arrive calm.

items.label: On arrival
items.detail: Freshen up, do a quick mirror check, then switch your attention to the conversation.

cards.question: Maham is the main speaker at Tuesday's client presentation. Her team usually wears business casual. What is the best choice?
options: Dress one step up, such as adding a blazer, waistcoat or formal dupatta
Wear the most casual thing she owns so she looks relaxed
Wear wedding clothes so the client remembers her
Wear exactly the same as everyone, but with sports shoes
cards.explanation: Speakers and hosts usually dress one step more formal than the audience. It signals respect for the client and helps her feel confident at the front of the room.

cards.title: In the room or on camera
cards.caption: Video calls need a few extra choices.

items.label: Colours
items.right: Solid mid-tone colours work best; very bright white or pure black can lose detail

items.label: Patterns
items.left: Small stripes and checks are fine
items.right: Tiny stripes and tight checks can flicker on screen; choose plain fabric

items.label: What is seen
items.right: Mainly head and shoulders, but dress fully in case you need to stand

items.label: Accessories
items.right: Bangles or chains that clink can be loud on the microphone

items.label: Background
items.right: A tidy, plain background and light facing you

cards.back: Dress to the client's level or one step above. When unsure, business formal is safe.
Choose a well-fitting outfit you can move in, in a calm colour that does not distract from your message.
Many Pakistani offices welcome neat shalwar kameez on Fridays. Keep it pressed; add a waistcoat if clients are visiting.
Festive local wear is welcome. Follow the invitation and avoid outshining the couple's family.
Smart casual or neat local wear usually fits. Check the invitation and venue.
Closed shoes, covered arms and legs, and any PPE the site provides. Safety comes before style.

cards.title: Weddings and office events
cards.body:
Office events and colleagues' weddings mix work and personal life, so they need a little thought.

- **Read the invitation.** It may say 'formal', 'traditional' or give a colour theme for a function such as a mehndi.
- **Festive, but suitable.** Colourful local wear, embroidered kurtas, a sherwani or a formal suit can all fit a wedding. Very revealing or very casual clothes usually do not.
- **Remember who is there.** Your manager and colleagues will see you, so stay within what feels respectful for a work relationship.
- **Comfort for long evenings.** Weddings can run late; choose shoes and fabrics you can wear for hours.
- **Office parties:** if the invitation says 'smart casual', a neat kurta or shirt is usually right. Avoid anything you would be uncomfortable seeing in a work photo.

cards.title: The Friday client visit
cards.situation: It is Friday. Omer, interning at Danish's print shop, has come in a neat shalwar kameez as usual. At 11 a.m. Danish says a corporate client will visit at 3 p.m. to approve a big printing order, and Omer will show them the samples.

choices.text: Keep his pressed shalwar kameez, add the waistcoat he keeps at the shop, and make sure his shoes are clean.
choices.outcome: Omer looks smart and respectful in local wear. The client is impressed by the neat team and the order is approved. A waistcoat is a simple way to step up.

choices.text: Rush home to change into a suit and tie.
choices.outcome: He makes it back just in time but flustered, and misses preparing the samples. Shalwar kameez can be formal enough with the right care.

choices.text: Stay as he is, with his sleeves rolled up and a crumpled collar from the morning's work.
choices.outcome: The client notices the untidy look at once. Fridays may be relaxed, but client visits still need neat attire.

cards.title: Good on camera?
cards.prompt: Sort each choice for a video call.

items.text: A plain, mid-tone shirt or kameez
A shirt with very fine, tight stripes
A neat top half and pyjama trousers below
Light facing you and a tidy background
Bangles that clink against the desk
A full, neat outfit even though only your shoulders show

cards.title: Abroad, ask first
cards.prompt: Match each travel situation to a sensible attire step.

pairs.left: A meeting in a country with more formal business norms
pairs.right: Pack business formal wear and check with your host

pairs.left: Visiting a place of worship while travelling
pairs.right: Cover arms, legs and, where asked, your head; follow posted guidance

pairs.left: A cold-weather conference
pairs.right: Pack warm, neat layers such as a dark coat and scarf

pairs.left: A country where some dress is restricted in public
pairs.right: Read official travel advice and the host company's guidance before you go

pairs.left: A long flight straight to a meeting
pairs.right: Wear crease-resistant clothes or change on arrival

cards.question: Maham has a video call with a partner abroad. Which top is the safest choice for the camera?
options: A shirt with very fine, tight stripes
A shiny sequinned top that reflects light
A bright white top under strong light
A plain mid-tone kameez or shirt without fine patterns
cards.explanation: Plain mid-tone fabric shows well on most cameras. Fine stripes can flicker, shiny fabrics reflect light, and very bright white can lose detail.

cards.title: Pack for a three-day business trip
cards.prompt: Put these packing steps in a sensible order.
steps: Check the schedule: meetings, events, site visits and free time
Research the dress norms and weather at the destination
Plan outfits around two or three neutral colours that mix
Choose crease-resistant fabrics and one versatile layer
Pack shoes, grooming kit and any PPE needed for site visits
Keep one meeting outfit in your hand luggage

cards.title: Maham's week, outfit by outfit
cards.body:
**Tuesday, client presentation:** her navy kurta and grey trousers with a formal dupatta and a fitted blazer. Calm colours, nothing to distract, and she can move easily at the front.

**Thursday, video call with Dubai:** a plain mid-blue kameez, neat hijab pinned securely, simple earrings that do not clink, a tidy background and light facing her.

**Friday, talk at Danish's shop:** a pressed cotton suit with closed flats, because the talk includes a walk past the printing machines.

**Saturday, colleague's mehndi:** a festive yellow outfit that fits the invitation's colour theme, comfortable shoes for a long evening, and nothing that outshines the bride's family.

cards.title: Working abroad or with foreign visitors
cards.body:
- **Research first:** read the host company's guidance and official travel advice, and ask your contacts what people normally wear.
- **Respect local norms,** especially at religious sites and in conservative places.
- **Your own dress is welcome too.** Many people proudly wear shalwar kameez or other national dress at international events where it suits the occasion.
- **Weather matters:** a Lahore summer outfit will not work in a European winter.
- Rules and customs can change, so check current guidance close to your trip.

cards.title: Take-aways from The Event Hall
items: Use the occasion check: who, where, what, weather and your work role.
For interviews, dress one step above the company's daily code and prepare days ahead.
Speakers and hosts usually dress one step more formal than the audience.
On video, choose plain mid-tone colours, avoid fine patterns and noisy jewellery, and dress fully.
Fridays and events may be relaxed or festive, but client visits and work photos still need care.
Before travel, research local norms, weather and official guidance, and keep a meeting outfit in hand luggage.

cards.prompt: Think of an event in your next month: an interview, meeting, call or celebration. Run the occasion check. What will you wear, and what will you prepare the night before?

quiz.question: Which five questions make up the occasion check in this stage?
options: Price, brand, trend, colour and season
When, why, how, how long and how much
Who, where, what, weather and work role
Size, shape, height, weight and age
quiz.explanation: The occasion check looks at the people, the place, the purpose, the weather and your role in the event.

quiz.question: For a job interview, what is a good general rule?
options: Dress two steps below so you look relaxed
Dress one step above the company's daily dress code
Always wear the most expensive outfit you own
Copy what the receptionist wore last year
quiz.explanation: One step above the usual code shows respect and preparation without looking out of place.

quiz.question: Why can a shirt with very fine, tight stripes be a problem on a video call?
options: Stripes are banned on most video platforms
The pattern can flicker or shimmer on many cameras
Stripes make the call drop more often
Cameras turn stripes into a different colour
quiz.explanation: Very fine patterns can create a flickering effect on camera. Plain fabrics are safer.

quiz.question: Omer is wearing a neat shalwar kameez on Friday when a client visit is announced. What is the simplest way to step up?
options: Add a waistcoat and check that his clothes and shoes are clean and pressed
Go home and change into a full suit and tie, even if it means missing the sample preparation
Roll up his sleeves to look hardworking
Change into sports clothes so he looks energetic
quiz.explanation: A pressed shalwar kameez with a waistcoat is a smart, respectful look in Pakistan. Preparation time matters too.

quiz.question: Why should you dress fully for a video call, even if only your shoulders show?
options: Most video platforms can detect your whole outfit and report it to the meeting host
It is required by law in every country
You may need to stand up, and it helps you act professional
The camera always shows the whole room
quiz.explanation: You may need to stand, fetch something or switch cameras. Dressing fully also helps your mindset.

quiz.question: What is a respectful choice for a colleague's wedding?
options: Your plainest office uniform, so that nobody can say you are trying to draw attention
The same outfit as the bride
Gym clothes, because weddings are long
Festive attire that fits the invitation without outshining the couple's family
quiz.explanation: Weddings welcome festive clothes. Follow the invitation and remember that colleagues and managers will see you.

quiz.question: Maham is the speaker at a client presentation; her team wears business casual. Which choice fits best?
options: Business casual plus one formal layer, such as a blazer or formal dupatta
Pure casual clothes, so that she looks approachable and the clients feel relaxed with her
Heavy party wear to stand out
Clothes she has never tried on before
quiz.explanation: A speaker usually dresses one step more formal than the audience, in clothes that fit and allow easy movement.

quiz.question: Before a work trip to a country you have not visited, which source is most useful for dress norms?
options: A single holiday photo from a friend
A fashion advert from that country
Guessing based on the weather only
The host company's guidance and official travel advice
quiz.explanation: Host guidance and official advice give reliable, up-to-date information. Customs and rules can change, so check close to the trip.

quiz.question: Why keep one meeting outfit in your hand luggage on a business trip?
options: Airlines require business travellers to carry one formal outfit in their hand luggage
Hand luggage keeps clothes crease-free forever
Checked luggage is always lost
If checked luggage is delayed, you can still attend the meeting looking prepared
quiz.explanation: Delayed bags happen. A meeting outfit in hand luggage protects your most important appointment.

quiz.question: On a visit to a client's factory, which attire choice matters most?
options: Closed shoes, covered arms and legs, and any PPE the site provides
A formal suit with open sandals, because clients notice the suit more than the shoes
Loose flowing clothes for comfort
Bright jewellery so people can see you
quiz.explanation: On a factory floor, safety comes before style. Follow the site rules and wear the PPE provided.

sessions.title: Cultural and Religious Sensitivity, Modesty and Inclusion
sessions.summary: Learn to respect the many ways colleagues dress for faith, culture, health and personal choice, including hijab, abaya, beards, turbans and more. Understand why we never judge appearance or bodies, how modesty means different things to different people, and what makes a dress code fair to all genders.
objectives: Respect religious and cultural dress such as hijab, abaya, beards, turbans and kara
Avoid comments on bodies, weight, skin colour and looks at work
Explain why modesty is a personal choice that should never be forced either way
Recognise what makes a dress code fair to all genders, faiths and abilities
Respond well when you or someone else makes an insensitive remark

cards.title: A joke that was not funny
cards.setting: A meeting room at Danish's print shop in Faisalabad. Jaspal is visiting to discuss a printing job for his company.

lines.text: Stage five. A friendly meeting takes a wrong turn, and Omer has to decide what to do.
Jaspal sahib, welcome. Omer will show you the proofs for your safety signs.
A visiting salesman, waiting for Danish, laughs and says loudly: 'Sardar ji, do you sleep in that turban too?' The room goes quiet.
My dastaar is part of my faith. I am happy to explain it another time. Shall we look at the proofs?
Jaspal sahib handled it calmly. But I wanted to say something and did not know what.
Later I spoke to the salesman privately. In this shop, we do not joke about anyone's faith, clothes or body. That is part of our dress etiquette too.
Respecting what others wear is as important as choosing what you wear. Let us learn how.

cards.title: Five habits of an inclusive workplace

scenes.heading: Notice without judging
scenes.narration: People dress for faith, culture, health, comfort and personal style. Notice the person and their work, not their clothes or body.

scenes.heading: Skip comments on bodies
scenes.narration: Do not comment on weight, height, skin colour or looks, even as a 'compliment'. It can hurt and is rarely about the work.

scenes.heading: Respect faith-based dress
scenes.narration: Hijab, abaya, niqab, beards, turbans, kara, skullcaps, crosses and other items are personal and protected by respect.

scenes.heading: Ask kindly, only if needed
scenes.narration: If you genuinely need to know something, such as safety fit, ask privately and politely. Do not make someone explain their faith for fun.

scenes.heading: Speak up for others
scenes.narration: If someone is mocked, support them. A calm 'Let us keep this respectful' changes the room.

cards.title: Judging or respecting?
cards.caption: Small changes in words make a big difference.

items.label: About a hijab
items.left: 'Why do you cover? It must be so hot.'
items.right: Treat it as normal; talk about the work

items.label: About weight
items.right: Say nothing about bodies

items.label: About skin colour
items.right: Never link skin colour to beauty or worth

items.label: About a beard or turban
items.right: Use the person's name and treat their choice as normal

items.label: About someone's outfit
items.right: If attire is a real policy issue, a manager raises it privately

cards.question: A new colleague wears an abaya and hijab. A team member keeps asking her why, in front of others. What is the best response?
options: Join in, because questions are always harmless
Tell the new colleague she should dress like everyone else
Gently steer the talk back to work and later tell the team member privately that this is personal
Report the new colleague for being different
cards.explanation: Repeated public questions about faith-based dress can make someone feel singled out. Redirect kindly, and speak to the questioner privately.

cards.back: A headscarf many Muslim women choose to wear. It can be worn in many styles. Treat it as a normal part of a person's attire.
A loose outer garment some women wear over their clothes. It can be fully professional, especially in plain colours.
A turban worn by Sikh men and some women as an article of faith. It should never be joked about or asked to be removed.
A steel bracelet worn by many Sikhs as an article of faith.
Many men keep beards for religious or cultural reasons, or by choice. A groomed beard is professional.
A small cap worn by some Muslim men and, in other forms, by people of other faiths, such as the Jewish kippah.

cards.title: Modesty is personal, both ways
cards.body:
Modesty means different things to different people. For some it means covering the head or wearing loose clothes; for others it means something else. Both are valid.

Three rules keep the workplace fair:

1. **No forcing.** No one should be pressured to cover more than they choose, or to remove a head covering, beard or other faith item to fit in.
2. **No judging.** Do not label colleagues as 'too modern' or 'too conservative' because of what they wear.
3. **Same standard of neatness for all.** A dress code can ask everyone to be clean, neat and suitable, while leaving room for faith, culture and health.

cards.title: What makes a dress code fair to all
cards.caption: A fair code passes all five tests.

items.label: Same level for all genders
items.detail: Men and women are asked for the same level of formality, not stricter rules for one.

items.label: No extra burden
items.detail: One group is not required to spend more, such as compulsory make-up or heels.

items.label: Faith and culture allowed
items.detail: Hijab, abaya, beards, turbans and similar items are allowed, with safety solutions where needed.

items.label: Health and disability
items.detail: Room for medical needs, such as comfortable shoes, no tie or adapted clothing.

items.label: Clear reasons
items.detail: Each rule has a reason: safety, hygiene, client contact or representing the organisation.

cards.title: Speaking up in the meeting
cards.situation: In a team meeting, a colleague says to Maham: 'With that hijab, you will never be sent to meet the foreign clients.' A few people laugh. Maham looks uncomfortable.

choices.text: Omer calmly says, 'Maham is our best presenter. Let us keep this respectful,' and later suggests she can report it to HR if she wants to.
choices.outcome: The laughter stops, Maham feels supported, and the comment is not repeated. Calm support plus a path to HR is the strongest response.

choices.text: Omer says nothing in the meeting but quietly checks on Maham afterwards.
choices.outcome: Maham appreciates the support, but the room learned that such comments pass without challenge. Checking in is good; speaking up as well is better.

choices.text: Omer laughs along so he does not look awkward.
choices.outcome: Maham feels isolated and the colleague thinks the remark was fine. Laughing along makes the problem bigger.

cards.title: Respectful or not?
cards.prompt: Sort each comment or action.

items.text: Talking to a colleague about their work, not their clothes
Saying someone 'would look better if they lost weight'
Giving a nickname based on someone's beard or turban
Offering a quiet room for prayer if the office has one
Telling a colleague her dupatta is 'old-fashioned'
Using a colleague's correct name and title
Linking fair skin with being more 'presentable'

cards.title: Inclusive responses
cards.prompt: Match each situation to a fair and respectful response.

pairs.left: A colleague needs a safety helmet that fits over a turban
pairs.right: Find a safe option together that respects the turban

pairs.left: A pregnant colleague cannot wear the uniform blazer comfortably
pairs.right: Offer a comfortable, adapted version of the uniform

pairs.left: A colleague with a foot condition needs soft shoes
pairs.right: Allow suitable shoes as a medical adjustment

pairs.left: A visitor asks a colleague to remove her hijab for a photo
pairs.right: Explain politely that it is her choice and is not removed

pairs.left: A team plans a dress theme for an event
pairs.right: Make it optional and easy to join with clothes people already have

cards.question: Which dress code rule is fair to all genders?
options: Women must wear make-up and heels; men have no extra rules
Everyone wears clean, neat business casual; options are listed by outfit, not by gender
Only men may wear local dress on client days
Women must cover more than they choose to
cards.explanation: A fair code asks the same level of neatness and formality from everyone, without extra costs or rules for one group, and leaves room for faith and personal choice.

cards.title: When you get it wrong
cards.prompt: If you make an insensitive remark about someone's appearance, put these steps in a good order.
steps: Stop and notice the effect of your words
Apologise sincerely and briefly, without excuses
Do not ask the person to comfort you or explain their faith
Learn more on your own about why it was hurtful
Change how you speak in future

cards.title: A global team call
cards.body:
Maham's company works with partners in Malaysia, the United Kingdom and the Gulf. On a video call, she sees one partner in a hijab and a business suit, another in a turban and blazer, a third in a short-sleeved shirt, and a fourth in a traditional dress from her own country.

Each is dressed suitably for their own workplace and culture. Nobody comments on anyone's clothes. The meeting is about the project.

Maham wears her usual neat kameez, blazer and hijab. 'I used to worry I would not look right for international calls,' she tells Farah. 'Now I see that professional looks different everywhere. Neat, respectful and confident is what counts.'

cards.title: Compliments: keep them about effort and work
cards.body:
Even kind comments on bodies can make people uncomfortable at work. If you want to be positive, focus on effort and work:

- 'Your presentation was very clear.'
- 'You always look well prepared for client meetings.'

Avoid comments about weight, shape, height, skin colour or attractiveness, and never comment on someone's body in front of others.

cards.title: Take-aways from The Open Courtyard
items: People dress for faith, culture, health and choice; respect all of them.
Never comment on bodies, weight, skin colour or attractiveness at work.
Modesty is personal: no forcing people to cover more or less than they choose.
A fair dress code asks the same of all genders, adds no extra burden and allows faith items.
Speak up calmly when someone is mocked, and offer support and a path to HR.
If you get it wrong, apologise briefly, learn and change.

cards.prompt: Think of a time you heard a comment about someone's clothes, body or faith at work or university. How did it affect the person? What could you say next time to keep things respectful?

quiz.question: Which item is worn by many Sikhs as an article of faith?
options: A coloured tie
A company lanyard
A wristwatch
The dastaar (turban) and the kara (steel bracelet)
quiz.explanation: The dastaar and the kara are articles of Sikh faith and should be respected, never mocked or removed for convenience.

quiz.question: What is the best way to give a positive comment at work?
options: Comment kindly on someone's weight loss in a meeting so the whole team can share the praise
Tell someone they would look better with fairer skin
Focus on effort and work, such as 'Your presentation was very clear'
Rate colleagues' looks in the team chat
quiz.explanation: Comments on bodies and looks can hurt, even when meant kindly. Comments on work and effort are safe and encouraging.

quiz.question: What does 'modesty is personal, both ways' mean?
options: Everyone must wear the same head covering
Only managers decide what is modest
No one should be pressured to cover more, or less, than they choose
Modesty rules apply only to women
quiz.explanation: Respect means not forcing anyone to change their choice in either direction, while keeping a shared standard of neatness.

quiz.question: Which rule in a dress code is unfair?
options: All staff wear clean, neat business casual
Closed shoes are required on the factory floor for everyone
Hijab, turbans and beards are welcome
Make-up and heels for women only
quiz.explanation: Rules that place extra cost or effort on one gender are unfair. A fair code asks the same level from everyone.

quiz.question: A colleague says to Maham in a meeting that her hijab will stop her meeting foreign clients. Others laugh. What is the strongest response from a teammate?
options: Laugh along to keep the mood light, then quietly tell Maham afterwards not to take it personally
Calmly ask to keep it respectful, then check on her
Tell Maham to stop wearing a hijab for client meetings
Ignore it completely and never mention it
quiz.explanation: Calm support in the moment, followed by a private check-in and a path to HR, protects the colleague and sets a clear standard.

quiz.question: A worker needs a safety helmet that works with his turban. What is the fair approach?
options: Tell him to remove the turban on site
Move him to a lower-paid role
Work with him to find a safe option that respects the turban
Let him work without any head protection
quiz.explanation: Safety and faith can both be respected. Employers should look for suitable options together with the worker and follow the safety rules that apply.

quiz.question: You made a careless joke about a colleague's clothes. What should you do?
options: Explain at length why it was only a joke and that they should not be so sensitive about it
Apologise briefly and sincerely, without excuses, and change how you speak
Ask the colleague to explain their culture so you understand
Pretend it never happened
quiz.explanation: A short, sincere apology and changed behaviour repair trust. Long excuses or asking the person to educate you add to the burden.

quiz.question: Why is linking fair skin with being 'more presentable' harmful at work?
options: It judges people by skin colour, which has nothing to do with their professionalism
Because skin colour can look different under office lights, which confuses people in meetings
Because it is only harmful in other countries
Because it is a fashion trend that has passed
quiz.explanation: Skin colour is not part of professional attire. Comments like this are a form of bias and hurt people's dignity.

quiz.question: A pregnant employee finds the uniform blazer uncomfortable. What is the best response from the employer?
options: Insist she wears the standard blazer
Ask her to stay home until after the birth
Tell her colleagues to comment on her size
Offer a comfortable, adapted version of the uniform
quiz.explanation: Fair dress codes make room for health needs. An adapted uniform keeps her comfortable and still represents the organisation.

quiz.question: On a global video call, partners wear a hijab with a suit, a turban with a blazer and a traditional national dress. What does this show about professional attire?
options: Only one international standard of dress is professional
Professional looks different across cultures
Faith-based dress is not suitable for global business
Everyone should copy the most senior person's clothes
quiz.explanation: There is no single global uniform. Neatness, suitability and respect for each other's choices make attire professional.

sessions.title: Attire Ethics for Managers and HR: Fair Codes, Private Feedback and PPE
sessions.summary: Step into the manager's and HR role. Write a dress code that is clear, fair and has a reason for every rule, communicate it well, give feedback on attire privately and respectfully, and make sure safety clothing and PPE protect everyone, including people who wear faith-based items.
objectives: Write a dress code with a clear reason for every rule
Communicate a dress code clearly to new and existing staff
Give feedback on attire privately, specifically and respectfully
Match attire rules to safety risk and client contact in different roles
Apply PPE rules consistently while respecting faith and health needs

cards.title: The dress code nobody understood
cards.setting: Danish's office above the print shop in Faisalabad. Farah joins by video from Karachi.

lines.text: Final stage. Danish's business has grown to twenty staff, and his one-line dress code is causing trouble.
Farah ji, my notice says only 'Dress decently'. One worker came in torn jeans, another was told off by a supervisor for her abaya. Now people are upset.
'Decently' means different things to different people. A good dress code explains what, why and how, and treats everyone the same.
And on the machine floor, it must start with safety. At our sites the PPE rules come first and apply to everyone.
And the worker in torn jeans? I did not want to embarrass him.
Good instinct. That conversation must be private and kind. Today we will write the code and plan that talk together.

scenes.heading: Purpose first
scenes.narration: Every rule needs a reason: safety, hygiene, client contact or representing the organisation. If a rule has no reason, drop it.

scenes.heading: Fair to everyone
scenes.narration: Rules apply equally to all genders and levels, allow faith and cultural dress, and leave room for health and disability needs.

scenes.heading: Clear and shared
scenes.narration: Write it simply, give examples, share it at joining and when it changes, and in the languages staff understand.

scenes.heading: Feedback in private
scenes.narration: Speak to one person privately and respectfully about the policy, never about their body, and listen to their reasons.

scenes.heading: Safety is not optional
scenes.narration: Where there is risk, PPE and safe clothing apply to everyone, consistently, with solutions for faith and health needs.

cards.title: Build a fair dress code in six steps
cards.caption: A code built this way is easier to follow and to defend.

items.label: Map the roles
items.detail: List roles by safety risk and client contact.

items.label: Set the purpose
items.detail: Write down why attire matters for each role group.

items.label: Draft with options
items.detail: Describe outfits by type, not by gender, with Western and local examples.

items.label: Check for fairness
items.detail: Test against faith, gender, health, disability and cost.

items.label: Consult and share
items.detail: Ask staff for feedback, then publish it clearly, in Urdu and English if needed.

items.label: Review and apply
items.detail: Apply it consistently and review it at least once a year or when work changes.
